- [ ] Forward descendancy versus reverse genealogy — known ancestor and bounded research question — Start reverse research with the subject and prove each parent-child link independently.|For descendancy, enumerate every child of the anchor couple before following grandchildren.|Expand one generation at a time with a queue; mark unresolved branches instead of silently dropping them.|Record spouses, adopted relationships, half relationships and dates separately from biological links.|Stop a branch only with a documented death/no-issue conclusion or an explicit unresolved status. — generation-by-generation lineage ledger

- [ ] Collateral lines and brickwalls — unresolved parentage or migration — Build a sibling set from censuses, probate distributions and household records.|Track witnesses, neighbors, sponsors and executors as an associates cluster.|Search each sibling in the destination jurisdiction and compare origin locations.|Test the proposed relationship against contradictory ages, occupations and simultaneous residences.|Write competing hypotheses and the next record that could discriminate them. — hypothesis table with exclusion evidence

- [ ] GPS and conflicting evidence — all competing assertions about one event — Define reasonably exhaustive research by jurisdiction, period and surviving record classes.|Cite repository, collection, volume, page/image, record identifier and access date.|Separate original versus derivative source from primary versus secondary information and direct versus indirect evidence.|Assess each informant’s opportunity to know; do not decide by majority vote among copied trees.|Resolve conflicting dates with event proximity, independent corroboration and calendar context.|Write a reasoned conclusion preserving unresolved contradictions. — proof argument and source matrix

- [ ] Same name, different person — candidate identities — Normalize names but retain exact spellings and aliases.|Compare time intervals, addresses, spouses, children, occupations and associates.|Reject impossible overlapping life histories; permit uncertain dates as intervals.|Require independent discriminators beyond a shared name before merging.|Keep a reversible merge ledger with provenance and rejected candidates. — identity resolution decision

- [ ] Forward descendancy versus reverse genealogy — known ancestor and bounded research question — Start reverse research with the subject and prove each parent-child link independently.|For descendancy, enumerate every child of the anchor couple before following grandchildren.|Expand one generation at a time with a queue; mark unresolved branches instead of silently dropping them.|Record spouses, adopted relationships, half relationships and dates separately from biological links.|Stop a branch only with a documented death/no-issue conclusion or an explicit unresolved status. — generation-by-generation lineage ledger

- [ ] Collateral lines and brickwalls — unresolved parentage or migration — Build a sibling set from censuses, probate distributions and household records.|Track witnesses, neighbors, sponsors and executors as an associates cluster.|Search each sibling in the destination jurisdiction and compare origin locations.|Test the proposed relationship against contradictory ages, occupations and simultaneous residences.|Write competing hypotheses and the next record that could discriminate them. — hypothesis table with exclusion evidence

- [ ] GPS and conflicting evidence — all competing assertions about one event — Define reasonably exhaustive research by jurisdiction, period and surviving record classes.|Cite repository, collection, volume, page/image, record identifier and access date.|Separate original versus derivative source from primary versus secondary information and direct versus indirect evidence.|Assess each informant’s opportunity to know; do not decide by majority vote among copied trees.|Resolve conflicting dates with event proximity, independent corroboration and calendar context.|Write a reasoned conclusion preserving unresolved contradictions. — proof argument and source matrix

- [ ] Same name, different person — candidate identities — Normalize names but retain exact spellings and aliases.|Compare time intervals, addresses, spouses, children, occupations and associates.|Reject impossible overlapping life histories; permit uncertain dates as intervals.|Require independent discriminators beyond a shared name before merging.|Keep a reversible merge ledger with provenance and rejected candidates. — identity resolution decision

- [ ] Forward descendancy versus reverse genealogy — known ancestor and bounded research question — Start reverse research with the subject and prove each parent-child link independently.|For descendancy, enumerate every child of the anchor couple before following grandchildren.|Expand one generation at a time with a queue; mark unresolved branches instead of silently dropping them.|Record spouses, adopted relationships, half relationships and dates separately from biological links.|Stop a branch only with a documented death/no-issue conclusion or an explicit unresolved status. — generation-by-generation lineage ledger

- [ ] Collateral lines and brickwalls — unresolved parentage or migration — Build a sibling set from censuses, probate distributions and household records.|Track witnesses, neighbors, sponsors and executors as an associates cluster.|Search each sibling in the destination jurisdiction and compare origin locations.|Test the proposed relationship against contradictory ages, occupations and simultaneous residences.|Write competing hypotheses and the next record that could discriminate them. — hypothesis table with exclusion evidence

- [ ] GPS and conflicting evidence — all competing assertions about one event — Define reasonably exhaustive research by jurisdiction, period and surviving record classes.|Cite repository, collection, volume, page/image, record identifier and access date.|Separate original versus derivative source from primary versus secondary information and direct versus indirect evidence.|Assess each informant’s opportunity to know; do not decide by majority vote among copied trees.|Resolve conflicting dates with event proximity, independent corroboration and calendar context.|Write a reasoned conclusion preserving unresolved contradictions. — proof argument and source matrix

- [ ] Same name, different person — candidate identities — Normalize names but retain exact spellings and aliases.|Compare time intervals, addresses, spouses, children, occupations and associates.|Reject impossible overlapping life histories; permit uncertain dates as intervals.|Require independent discriminators beyond a shared name before merging.|Keep a reversible merge ledger with provenance and rejected candidates. — identity resolution decision

- [ ] Forward descendancy versus reverse genealogy — known ancestor and bounded research question — Start reverse research with the subject and prove each parent-child link independently.|For descendancy, enumerate every child of the anchor couple before following grandchildren.|Expand one generation at a time with a queue; mark unresolved branches instead of silently dropping them.|Record spouses, adopted relationships, half relationships and dates separately from biological links.|Stop a branch only with a documented death/no-issue conclusion or an explicit unresolved status. — generation-by-generation lineage ledger

- [ ] Collateral lines and brickwalls — unresolved parentage or migration — Build a sibling set from censuses, probate distributions and household records.|Track witnesses, neighbors, sponsors and executors as an associates cluster.|Search each sibling in the destination jurisdiction and compare origin locations.|Test the proposed relationship against contradictory ages, occupations and simultaneous residences.|Write competing hypotheses and the next record that could discriminate them. — hypothesis table with exclusion evidence

- [ ] GPS and conflicting evidence — all competing assertions about one event — Define reasonably exhaustive research by jurisdiction, period and surviving record classes.|Cite repository, collection, volume, page/image, record identifier and access date.|Separate original versus derivative source from primary versus secondary information and direct versus indirect evidence.|Assess each informant’s opportunity to know; do not decide by majority vote among copied trees.|Resolve conflicting dates with event proximity, independent corroboration and calendar context.|Write a reasoned conclusion preserving unresolved contradictions. — proof argument and source matrix

- [ ] Same name, different person — candidate identities — Normalize names but retain exact spellings and aliases.|Compare time intervals, addresses, spouses, children, occupations and associates.|Reject impossible overlapping life histories; permit uncertain dates as intervals.|Require independent discriminators beyond a shared name before merging.|Keep a reversible merge ledger with provenance and rejected candidates. — identity resolution decision

- [ ] Forward descendancy versus reverse genealogy — known ancestor and bounded research question — Start reverse research with the subject and prove each parent-child link independently.|For descendancy, enumerate every child of the anchor couple before following grandchildren.|Expand one generation at a time with a queue; mark unresolved branches instead of silently dropping them.|Record spouses, adopted relationships, half relationships and dates separately from biological links.|Stop a branch only with a documented death/no-issue conclusion or an explicit unresolved status. — generation-by-generation lineage ledger

- [ ] Collateral lines and brickwalls — unresolved parentage or migration — Build a sibling set from censuses, probate distributions and household records.|Track witnesses, neighbors, sponsors and executors as an associates cluster.|Search each sibling in the destination jurisdiction and compare origin locations.|Test the proposed relationship against contradictory ages, occupations and simultaneous residences.|Write competing hypotheses and the next record that could discriminate them. — hypothesis table with exclusion evidence

- [ ] GPS and conflicting evidence — all competing assertions about one event — Define reasonably exhaustive research by jurisdiction, period and surviving record classes.|Cite repository, collection, volume, page/image, record identifier and access date.|Separate original versus derivative source from primary versus secondary information and direct versus indirect evidence.|Assess each informant’s opportunity to know; do not decide by majority vote among copied trees.|Resolve conflicting dates with event proximity, independent corroboration and calendar context.|Write a reasoned conclusion preserving unresolved contradictions. — proof argument and source matrix

- [ ] Same name, different person — candidate identities — Normalize names but retain exact spellings and aliases.|Compare time intervals, addresses, spouses, children, occupations and associates.|Reject impossible overlapping life histories; permit uncertain dates as intervals.|Require independent discriminators beyond a shared name before merging.|Keep a reversible merge ledger with provenance and rejected candidates. — identity resolution decision

- [ ] Indirect and negative evidence — missing or indirect record — Document the record’s coverage and whether the person should have appeared.|Distinguish a failed keyword query from an inspected complete record set.|Combine independent indirect assertions into a written logical chain.|Treat destroyed records and incomplete indexes as absence of evidence, not negative proof.|Record alternative explanations and a falsification search. — negative-search log

- [ ] Kinship degree and distribution — proved common ancestor and descent paths — Count parent-child edges from each person to the nearest shared ancestor.|For collateral cousins with depths a and b at least two: cousin degree=min(a,b)-1; removal=abs(a-b).|Depths 2/2 yield first cousins; 3/3 second cousins; 4/4 third cousins; 2/3 first cousins once removed.|Handle ancestors, siblings, half relationships and pedigree collapse explicitly rather than forcing the cousin formula.|Compute per stirpes and per capita shares only under the applicable jurisdiction’s actual representation rule; do not infer the statutory variant from the label.|Use rational fractions and verify distributions sum to one after spouse and other priority interests. — kinship chart plus jurisdiction-specific share worksheet

- [ ] Testate and intestate routing — death, domicile, assets and possible will — Locate the original will, codicils and any admission order; a found will is not necessarily an admitted will.|Identify domicile probate and any ancillary real-property proceedings.|Distinguish devisees under a valid will from intestate heirs and nonprobate beneficiaries.|Search prior administrations and reopened proceedings before opening a duplicate matter.|Build a jurisdiction/date-specific succession rule table. — estate route decision

- [ ] Probate lifecycle — case docket and jurisdiction — Extract petition, notice, service and hearing events with filed and effective dates.|Verify Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration, representative identity and limitations.|Capture bond, waivers, inventory and appraisement.|Track creditor notice, filing deadlines, allowed claims and payment priority from actual rules.|Reconcile interim/final accounting, sale orders and distributions.|Use the final decree and receipts to close the chain; do not substitute a petition for an adjudication. — dated event ledger and missing-document queue

- [ ] Guardianship and minor heirs — minor or incapacitated beneficiary — Identify guardianship/conservatorship separately from estate administration.|Read appointment orders for powers, bond and sale/distribution restrictions.|Do not treat a guardian’s personal signature as authority to sell a minor’s interest.|Track age-of-majority and successor fiduciary events.|Reconcile funds with court approval and final accounting. — authority matrix

- [ ] Unindexed probate packets — court, decedent variants and death interval — Search docket/index variants, then petition numbers and estate numbers.|Request the complete packet, not only the will.|Follow minute books, order books, inventories and loose-paper references.|Record gaps in page numbering and request missing exhibits.|Cross-check docket events against documents actually received. — packet completeness checklist

- [ ] Death-first research — subject identity and estimated death interval — Search death evidence first to bound the life timeline and locate the final jurisdiction.|Compare residence, place of death, place of burial and probate venue rather than assuming they match.|Use the informant and funeral home to generate family leads.|Move backward to marriage and birth only after stabilizing the death identity.|Record whether the certificate is original, amended, index-only or a later abstract. — death identity anchor

- [ ] Death certificate extraction — certificate image — Extract every field including informant name, relationship and address.|Capture burial place/date, undertaker, funeral home and disposition method.|Record cause and duration of illness as contextual clues, not identity proof alone.|Separate medical certifier knowledge from informant-supplied parentage.|Link each assertion to the page and field; preserve unknown and blank distinctly. — field-level death record table

- [ ] SSDI and SS-5 — death identity and Social Security clues — Search SSDI variants and compare dates with primary death records.|Distinguish death-index data from the original SS-5 application.|Evaluate lawful access and availability before requesting an application.|Use application parent names and birth details as assertions requiring corroboration.|Do not publish full sensitive identifiers in derived reports. — SSDI/SS-5 evidence comparison

- [ ] No certificate fallback ladder — documented failed civil death search — Search burial registers, cemetery sexton records and grave ownership.|Search applicable mortality schedules and coroner/inquest records.|Search church burial registers and funeral home files.|Search probate petitions, inventories and guardianship records.|Compare tax cessation, deed transitions and census disappearance without treating any one as a death date.|Bound the death interval between last-known-alive and first independently recorded death evidence. — bounded death interval with fallback citations

- [ ] Marriage and obituary chaining — names across multiple records — Build a dated surname timeline from marriages, divorces and remarriages.|Search maiden names, prior married names, initials and spouse names.|Extract survivors, predeceased relatives, residences, funeral details and relationship wording from obituaries.|Check newspaper issue date, edition, page and image; OCR search failures require browsing.|Do not equate omitted relatives with disinheritance or proof of no relationship. — surname alias graph and obituary family table
